rationale: A wins because it keeps finding the tension inside the facts, especially “Instacart's ad business hit a $1B run rate while its delivery growth stalled to single digits.” B has usable bones, but it turns the same fact set into a bigger thesis than the update earns: “business-model-pivot story” needs revenue mix, not just a shiny ad number. A still gets a little cute with “the grocery aisle's newest ad surface,” but it names the proof that would make or kill the angle; B too often treats missing proof as a premise.
gaps_in_A: “A cart that watches what you put in it is now the grocery aisle's newest ad surface” asserts cart ad inventory before the update says carts serve ads or feed ad targeting. The proof list cleans up the mess, but the headline still oversteps.
“a few hundred stores across a 1,500-plus banner network — meaning the vast majority of banners have not deployed them” does bad arithmetic. Stores and banners are not the same unit.
“this beat has already seen fail twice” is an unsupported wink. If you mean Amazon Go or prior smart-cart attempts, say so with evidence or cut it.
gaps_in_B: “business-model-pivot story” and “actual revenue model” overclaim. The update gives ad run rate and slowed delivery growth, not revenue mix or a strategic pivot.

“The $1B threshold is a widely recognized milestone in the retail media category” is an invented peg unless you bring external evidence. It sounds authoritative because it has a round number; that is not the same thing as proof.
“as digital attribution has gotten harder” imports a market narrative not supplied in the update. Maybe true, maybe useful, but it is not grounded here.

“a stated plan to grow across 1,500+ banner partners” overstates the rollout. The update says Instacart has 1,500 retail banners and plans to expand carts, not that carts are expanding across that whole base.
